newsitem.title: UK: Footballer Fashanu a hero on and off pitch-witness.
newsitem.headline: Footballer Fashanu a hero on and off pitch-witness.

text.p: Former England and Wimbledon striker John Fashanu declined to testify in his football match-rigging trial on Friday, but defence witnesseses described him as a hero on and off the pitch.

"We knew of the astonishing reputation he had in Africa both at a political level and with ordinary people," Robert Smith, executive director of the United Kingdom Committee for UNICEF, told the trial in the southern English city of Winchester.
Fashanu, accused of conspiring to give and accept money as inducements to influence the outcome of soccer matches, has exercised his right to silence throughout the high-profile trial.
He has denied the charges along with his co-defendants Zimbabwean-born, former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, Dutch keeper Hans Segers and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim.

Smith said Fashanu was UNICEF's "special ambassador for the children of Africa" and he praised the former goalkeeper-turned-television presenter for helping to rebuild the Zambian football team, which was killed in an air crash.

Director of football at Coventry City, Ron Atkinson, told the court about Fashanu's athletic prowess and described his aggression and competitiveness as just the right combination for the Aston Villa football team which he managed in 1994.

"He's a very, very confident person. I can remember him when he was about 14, I tried to sign him on schoolboy forms for Cambridge United. I followed his career all the way through, he's always given the impression that he's one of those that's wanted to make something of his life," he said.
Fashanu, who reached the peak of his fame as a soccer player with Wimbledon in the late 1980s, juggled his obligations to the club with a successful career as a media personality.
He presented a well-known television game show and acts as a special representative for the United Nations Children Fund (UNICEF) to Africa.
Abandoned by his Nigerian father, he and his footballing brother Justin were brought up by foster parents in eastern England.
He played twice for England in 1989 and 324 times for Wimbledon, scoring 129 times.
A knee injury forced him to retire in 1994, shortly after his move to Midlands side Aston Villa.
